name: Heroku
summary: The platform that defined PaaS: `git push` your code, and Heroku builds it with a buildpack and runs it on managed containers called dynos behind its own HTTP router.
intro: You push code to a Git remote named `heroku`. A buildpack detects the language from files such as `package.json` or `requirements.txt`, fetches dependencies and compiles the app into a build artifact: a slug (a tarball with the code and its runtime) on the older Cedar generation, an OCI image built by Cloud Native Buildpacks on the newer Fir generation. Heroku pairs the artifact with your config vars and add-ons into a numbered release, kept in an append-only ledger, so `heroku releases:rollback` starts an older one again. The dyno manager then runs each line of your `Procfile` (`web`, `worker` and so on) on dynos, isolated Linux containers, as many as you scale each process type to. Only `web` dynos get HTTP traffic: Heroku’s routers pick one at random for each request. Dynos are replaced on every deploy and cycled automatically (at least once a day unless configured otherwise), each with a fresh, ephemeral filesystem, so state lives in add-ons such as Heroku Postgres, whose credentials arrive as environment variables like `DATABASE_URL`.

Prices are per dyno. On the Common Runtime, Eco costs $5 a month for a pool of 1,000 dyno hours shared by all Eco dynos, which sleep after 30 minutes without traffic; Basic is $7 with 0.5 GB and one dyno per process type; Standard-1X (0.5 GB) and Standard-2X (1 GB) cost $25 and $50; single-tenant Performance dynos run from $250 (2.5 GB) to $1,500 (126 GB) and support autoscaling. Fir, rolled out from 2025 and generally available with Fir Private Spaces, runs dynos on Kubernetes on AWS (EKS), uses Cloud Native Buildpacks by default, offers x86 and ARM dynos and exports telemetry with OpenTelemetry.

Heroku is part of Salesforce. On February 6, 2026, it moved to a “sustaining engineering model” focused on stability, security, reliability and support rather than new features, and stopped offering Enterprise Account contracts to new customers; credit-card customers saw no change, and smaller releases, such as Heroku Postgres Advanced in October 2026, continue.
strengths: The whole deploy path is `git push`, with official buildpacks for Ruby, Node.js, Java, Python, Clojure, Scala, Go, PHP and .NET
Every change to code, config vars or add-ons is a numbered release, and rolling back is one command
The Elements Marketplace attaches databases, caches, logging and more as add-ons that hand the app their credentials in config vars
Fir builds standard OCI images with Cloud Native Buildpacks, and Heroku’s builder also runs locally with the `pack` CLI
limits: The router ends any request that takes longer than 30 seconds, and the limit can’t be changed: long work has to go to a worker dyno
Files written to a dyno vanish when it restarts, which happens on every deploy and on the regular, automatic dyno cycling
Eco and Basic dynos can’t scale out, and Eco dynos sleep after 30 minutes idle and take a few seconds to wake
Since February 2026 Heroku is in sustaining engineering: new Enterprise contracts are no longer sold, and the stated focus is stability over new features

snippet.title: Create, deploy, scale and roll back an app with the Heroku CLI
source: heroku create -a example-app             # empty app plus a Git remote named heroku
git push heroku main                     # buildpack build, new release, one web dyno
heroku ps:scale web=3 queue=2            # dyno formation per Procfile process type
heroku config:set ENCRYPTION_KEY=secret  # config var, exposed as an env var; new release
heroku addons:create heroku-redis:mini   # Key-Value Store add-on; sets REDIS_URL
heroku logs --ps web.1 --tail            # one dyno's log stream from Logplex
heroku releases:rollback v102            # run an earlier release again

story: Heroku began in June 2007, built by James Lindenbaum, Adam Wiggins and Orion Henry to run Ruby apps written for Rack. Heroku’s pitch, as Salesforce later put it, was “no virtual machines to manage, no software to install, and no hardware to manage and tune”: push the code and the platform does the rest. A rebuilt platform launched in January 2009.

Salesforce agreed to buy Heroku on December 8, 2010, for about $212 million, when it ran more than 105,000 apps. Heroku grew from Ruby into a polyglot platform: in 2011 it conceived buildpacks, open scripts that teach the build system a new language, and Wiggins wrote the twelve-factor app from what the team had seen across hundreds of thousands of apps. In 2018 Heroku and Pivotal started Cloud Native Buildpacks to make the idea a standard that outputs OCI images.

Heroku’s free dyno and data plans ended from November 28, 2022, with Heroku citing the effort spent on fraud and abuse. From 2025, Heroku rebuilt the platform as Fir, on Kubernetes, OCI images and OpenTelemetry. In February 2026 it moved to a sustaining engineering model, concentrating on keeping existing customers’ apps stable and secure.

choices.why: Developers already used Git, so Heroku made deploying “the familiar `git push`”, to a remote it adds when you create the app. GitHub integration and the Platform API are other ways to send it.

choices.choice: A Procfile of named process types
choices.why: Declaring `web` and `queue` as separate commands exposes the app’s architecture to the platform, so each part can be scaled on its own, and only `web` dynos get routed traffic.

A release binds a build to config vars and add-ons. Changing any of them makes a new release instead of editing the running one, which gives an audit trail and makes rollback a matter of starting an old release.
Heroku says Fir uses Kubernetes, OCI containers and OpenTelemetry to “future-proof” apps and fit modern cloud tooling, while keeping the Heroku workflow on top.

timeline.text: Development starts in June, for Ruby apps only
Salesforce agrees to buy Heroku for about $212 million on December 8
Heroku conceives buildpacks; Adam Wiggins writes the twelve-factor app
Heroku and Pivotal start Cloud Native Buildpacks
Free dynos and data plans end from November 28
Fir, the Kubernetes-based generation, begins rolling out
